Stochastic Sparse Attention for Memory-Bound Inference

Kyle Lee Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA, USA Correspondence to: kylelee@ucsb.edu    Corentin Delacour Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA, USA    Kevin Callahan-Coray Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA, USA    Kyle Jiang Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA, USA    Can Yaras Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA    Samet Oymak Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA    Tathagata Srimani Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA    Kerem Y. Camsari Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA, USA
Abstract

Autoregressive decoding becomes bandwidth-limited at long contexts, as generating each token requires reading all nkn_{k} key and value vectors from KV cache. We present Stochastic Additive No-mulT Attention (SANTA), a method that sparsifies value-cache access by sampling S≪nkS\ll n_{k} indices from the post-softmax distribution and aggregates only those value rows. This yields an unbiased estimator of the post-softmax value aggregation while replacing value-stage multiply-accumulates with gather-and-add. We introduce stratified sampling to design variance-reduced, GPU-friendly variants, demonstrating 1.5×1.5\times decode-step attention kernel speedup over FlashInfer and FlashDecoding on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada while matching baseline accuracy at 32k-token contexts. Finally, we propose Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} sampling as a complementary technique to sparsify the score stage, reducing key-feature access through stochastic ternary queries. Both methods are orthogonal to upstream techniques such as ternary quantization, low-rank projections, and KV-cache compression. Together, they point toward sparse, multiplier-free, and energy-efficient inference. We open-source our kernels at: https://github.com/OPUSLab/SANTA.git

Keywords: 
Large Language Models, Transformers, Attention, Monte Carlo methods, Sparse computation, Energy-efficient inference

1 Introduction

Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) underpin modern language models (OpenAI, 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Gemini Team et al., 2023). As deployments increasingly rely on long contexts, autoregressive decoding enters a regime where throughput is often limited by memory bandwidth: generating each new token repeatedly streams the Key–Value (KV) cache for all prior tokens. For example, for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at a 32k-token context, streaming bf16 keys and values is on the order of ∼\sim128 MB per layer per generated token, and KV memory demands scale linearly with context length and batch size.

A broad literature mitigates this bottleneck from several angles. KV-cache quantization/compression reduces bytes per element (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024); cache-management policies reduce the number of retained tokens (Tang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023); and structured sparsity or candidate selection reduces attention cost (Child et al., 2019; Zaheer et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Kitaev et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2025). Architectural changes such as grouped-query attention (GQA) reduce KV footprint by sharing keys/values across heads (Ainslie et al., 2023), and decoding kernels improve IO locality for exact attention (Dao et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2025). However, even with optimized exact kernels, long-context decoding still incurs a persistent cost: each step touches essentially the full KV state.

We study a complementary inference-time lever: reducing the amount of KV data accessed per decode step without permanently discarding cache contents. Our primary focus is the post-softmax value aggregation, where dense attention computes A​VAV by multiplying attention weights by all nkn_{k} value rows. We introduce Stochastic Additive No-mulT Attention (SANTA), which samples S≪nkS\ll n_{k} indices from the post-softmax distribution and aggregates only those sampled rows of VV via gather-and-add. This yields an unbiased estimator of the post-softmax value aggregation while reducing value-cache row reads per query from nkn_{k} to SS (and eliminating value-stage multiplications in favor of additive accumulation). We further propose variance-reduced variants (𝐒𝟐\mathbf{S^{2}}ANTA) based on stratified and systematic sampling that bolster accuracy and admit GPU-friendly implementations. Since sparsifying VV reads yields the clearest bandwidth benefit in decoding, our systems evaluation targets decode-step acceleration at long contexts.

On modern GPUs, these changes translate into measurable kernel-level gains: our S2S^{2}ANTA CUDA kernels achieve up to 1.5×\mathbf{1.5\times} decode-step attention-kernel speedup over FlashInfer and FlashDecoding at 32k-token contexts while matching baseline accuracy on long-context prompts (Section 3).

Finally, we propose Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} sampling as a complementary technique for the score stage: it represents query elements as Bernoulli variables to form sparse ternary queries in {−1,0,+1}\{-1,0,+1\}, yielding an unbiased estimator of q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} and inducing feature-sparse key access during decoding. In this work, our implemented kernels and measured speedups are driven primarily by value-stage sparsification; Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} is presented as a complementary mechanism that can be combined with SANTA to sparsify both branches.

Contributions. Concretely, we: (i) introduce SANTA and variance-reduced S2S^{2}ANTA as unbiased estimators of the post-softmax value aggregation that reduce value-cache reads from nkn_{k} to SS; (ii) design GPU kernels that parallelize sampling and sparse accumulation, demonstrating up to 1.5×1.5\times decode-step attention-kernel speedup over FlashInfer/FlashDecoding at 32k-token contexts while matching baseline accuracy; (iii) empirically characterize tunable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs on GSM8K, MMLU, and long-context benchmarks; and (iv) propose Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} sampling as a complementary score-stage estimator that can reduce key-feature access during decoding.

2 Stochastic Additive No-mulT Attention (SANTA)

In principle, SANTA can be employed for the prefill or decode stages. Since the benefit of sparse memory access becomes apparent in decode, we present SANTA as a decoding algorithm. In autoregressive decoding, we consider a single query vector q∈ℝ1×dkq\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{k}}. Scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) is expressed as a function of the key matrix and value matrix:

Attn​(q,K,V)=softmax​(q​K𝖳dk)​V=A​V,\text{Attn}(q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\left(\frac{qK^{\mathsf{T}}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V=AV, (1)

where K∈ℝnk×dkK\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}\times d_{k}} is the key matrix, V∈ℝnk×dkV\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}\times d_{k}} is the value matrix, and A∈ℝ1×nkA\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times n_{k}} represents the attention scores as a probability distribution.

To approximate A​VAV, we treat AA as a categorical distribution over keys and sample SS indices i.i.d. from it (with replacement). For query vector qq, we fetch the corresponding SS rows of VV and average them. This yields an estimate of the attention output using only row indexing and addition.

As an illustrative example, consider number of keys nk=3n_{k}=3. We sample S=3S=3 one-hot attention vectors from the categorical distribution AA:

A​V^=13​([100]+[100]+[001])​V,\widehat{AV}=\frac{1}{3}\left(\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\right)V, (2)

which simplifies by distributivity of matrix multiplication over addition:

A​V^\displaystyle\widehat{AV} =13​([100]​V+[100]​V+[001]​V)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{3}\left(\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\end{bmatrix}V+\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\end{bmatrix}V+\begin{bmatrix}0&0&1\end{bmatrix}V\right) (3)
=13​(V1+V1+V3).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{3}\bigl(V_{1}+V_{1}+V_{3}\bigr).

where each Vi∈ℝ1×dkV_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{k}} is a sampled row of VV. The one-hot attention vectors in Eqs. 2, 3 are only for illustrative purposes; they represent an indexing and gather operation, and are not materialized as vectors in memory.

Finally, SANTA can be summarized as:

A​V^=1S​∑s=1SVis≈A​V,\widehat{AV}=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}V_{i_{s}}\approx AV, (4)

where isi_{s} is a sampled index and each VisV_{i_{s}} denotes a gathered row from VV. Multiplications in the value stage have therefore been eliminated in favor of sampling, indexing and addition. If SS is chosen as a power of 2 (and the model has a fixed point representation), normalization may be implemented as a bit-shift. Fig. 1 illustrates SANTA’s memory access benefits for autoregressive decoding: SANTA sparsely reads only S≪nkS\ll n_{k} sampled rows of VV and computes an additive average without multiplications after the softmax.

We provide a formal mathematical description of SANTA in Appendix A. SANTA is an unbiased estimator of the attention function whose variance scales as 1/S1/S (Appendix A.1,  A.2). A dimension-free high-probability concentration bound for SANTA is deferred to Appendix B.

2.1 S2S^{2}ANTA: stratified and systematic sampling

S2S^{2}ANTA reduces variance via stratified sampling: dividing the CDF into SS equal probability mass intervals and sampling once per interval for better coverage of the attention distribution. We devise two variants: independent stratified sampling (𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-strat) and systematic sampling (𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-sys).

The mechanics of S2S^{2}ANTA-strat remain identical to default SANTA, except the SS samples are drawn per stratum instead of iid from the full distribution. Systematic sampling (𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-sys) similarly splits the attention distribution CDF into SS equal probability mass partitions. However, whereas independent stratified sampling draws SS random offsets for each of SS strata, systematic sampling draws a single offset UU and applies the same offset to all strata, effectively drawing SS samples with a single random number.

Construction.

Fix a query qq. Let Aq=(pq​1,…,pq​nk)A_{q}=(p_{q1},\dots,p_{qn_{k}}) be the attention weights and FqF_{q} the associated CDF on [0,1)[0,1). Partition [0,1)[0,1) into SS equal intervals

Im:=[m/S,(m+1)/S),m=0,…,S−1.I_{m}:=[m/S,(m+1)/S),\qquad m=0,\dots,S-1.

Define two schemes:

  • •

    Independent stratified (S𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-strat). Draw Tm∼Unif⁡(Im)T_{m}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(I_{m}) independently for m=0,…,S−1m=0,\dots,S-1, set Jm:=Fq−1​(Tm)J_{m}:=F_{q}^{-1}(T_{m}), and output A​V^qind:=1S​∑m=0S−1VJm.\widehat{AV}_{q}^{\mathrm{ind}}:=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{m=0}^{S-1}V_{J_{m}}.

  • •

    Systematic (S𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-sys). Draw a single U∼Unif⁡([0,1/S))U\sim\mathrm{Unif}([0,1/S)) and take thresholds Tm:=U+m/ST_{m}:=U+m/S. With Jm:=Fq−1​(Tm)J_{m}:=F_{q}^{-1}(T_{m}), output A​V^qsys:=1S​∑m=0S−1VJm.\widehat{AV}_{q}^{\mathrm{sys}}:=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{m=0}^{S-1}V_{J_{m}}.

𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-strat and 𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-sys are unbiased estimators of attention (see Appendix A.4). Only 𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-strat has a theoretical guarantee of variance reduction compared to default SANTA (see Appendix A.5). Despite lacking a variance reduction guarantee, we validate that 𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-sys exhibits comparable performance to 𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-strat on reasoning benchmarks and long-context benchmarks. 𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-sys demonstrates similar variance reduction to 𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-strat in practice (see Appendix D). Systematic sampling with 𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA-sys is appealing because it draws samples using one random number instead of SS random numbers, which may be easier to implement in hardware.

2.2 Theoretical operations and memory accesses

By virtue of SANTA’s sparsity, in autoregressive decoding, SANTA demonstrates a S/nkS/n_{k} reduction in post-softmax additions and reads to rows of VV, where SS is the sample budget and nkn_{k} is the number of keys. SANTA removes post-softmax multiplications in favor of additive accumulation (see Appendix E for analysis of decode-step operations and memory accesses).

In prefill, while similar arguments hold for SANTA’s reduced additions and removed multiplies, there is no longer sparse memory access to the value matrix VV. Each of nq=nkn_{q}=n_{k} queries may each sample SS rows of VV, therefore requiring ≫S\gg S rows of VV when the union across all queries is considered (see Appendices F, G for prefill analysis).

3 GPU kernels for variance-reduced SANTA

Section 2 introduced SANTA and variance-reduced sampling rules (stratified/systematic), which specify what to sample to form an unbiased estimator of the value-stage aggregation A​VAV. In this section we focus on how to realize these samplers efficiently at decode time on GPUs: we introduce two kernel strategies, S2S^{2}ANTA-prop and S2S^{2}ANTA-flash, which differ in how they allocate samples across tiles (global proportional allocation vs. speculative per-tile sampling with deferred normalization).

3.1 Parallelizing stochastic attention on GPUs

Efficient implementation on GPUs presents a unique systems challenge: parallelizing the sampling control flow. Standard attention (SDPA) is amenable to “split-KV” strategies (e.g., FlashDecoding (Dao et al., 2023)) because the reduction of values is associative: partial sums can be computed locally and merged later. Sampling, however, creates a sequential dependency: determining which rows of VV to access generally requires a global Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF). A naive implementation would require a sequential pass over the global probability distribution to draw sample indices, leaving the GPU compute units idle and preventing parallel access to the value matrix.

To unlock parallel VV-access, we must determine the number of samples per tile before or independently of the full global reduction. We propose two strategies to break this dependency:

  1. 1.

    Proportional Sample Allocation (S2S^{2}ANTA-prop): We pre-calculate the probability mass of each tile to deterministically assign sample budgets. This requires a global barrier but ensures exact load balancing.

  2. 2.

    Speculative Local Sampling (S2S^{2}ANTA-flash): Tiles sample independently with uniform budgets, speculating that all tiles are equally important, followed by a post-hoc re-weighting. This removes the barrier but introduces sample waste.

We implement both strategies and evaluate their decode-step kernel latency and long-context accuracy at 32k-token prompts in Section 3.4.

3.2 S2S^{2}ANTA-prop: exact budget allocation via global sync

S2S^{2}ANTA-prop (Figure 2) breaks the sequential sampling dependency by resolving the global partition function ZZ in a lightweight initial pass.

The algorithm proceeds in three stages. The key dimension nkn_{k} is partitioned into tiles of length BtileB_{\rm tile}.

  1. 1.

    Pass 1 (score stash & tile stats): We compute attention scores exactly. The exponentiated scores (or a normalized equivalent) are written to global memory. Crucially, since the scores are scalars (1×nk1\times n_{k}) while the values are vectors (nk×dkn_{k}\times d_{k}), this stash consumes negligible bandwidth (1/dk1/d_{k}) compared to a full value fetch. We also compute and write local partition functions ZtileZ_{\rm tile}.

  2. 2.

    Global budget allocation: A separate kernel sums the tile statistics to find the global ZZ. It then assigns a specific sample count to each tile: Stile∝S⋅(Ztile/Z)S_{\rm tile}\propto S\cdot(Z_{\rm tile}/Z).

  3. 3.

    Pass 2 (parallel gather): Using the stashed scores and the assigned StileS_{\rm tile}, each tile systematically samples indices and accumulates rows from VV. Tiles with low probability mass are assigned Stile=0S_{\rm tile}=0, allowing them to skip the expensive VV-read entirely.

Comprehensive pseudocode is in Appendix O.

3.3 S2S^{2}ANTA-flash: Speculative Sampling with Deferred Normalization

To eliminate the latency of the global synchronization barrier, S2S^{2}ANTA-flash (Figure 3) adopts a speculative approach structurally similar to FlashDecoding.

Instead of pre-calculating the global budget, each tile is allocated a fixed, uniform budget Stile≈S/TS_{\rm tile}\approx S/T, where TT is the number of tiles. Each tile samples locally as if it contained the entire probability mass. A second reduction kernel then computes the true global partition function ZZ and down-weights the partial outputs of tiles that had low probability mass.

This method maximizes parallelism by removing the global barrier but suffers from sample waste: tiles with low probability mass still consume compute and bandwidth to draw samples that are effectively down-weighted during the final merge. In our 32k-token evaluation (Section 3.4), matching SDPA accuracy requires substantially larger budgets for S2S^{2}ANTA-flash; the accuracy-matching operating point is S=2048S{=}2048 for S2S^{2}ANTA-flash versus S=128S{=}128 for S2S^{2}ANTA-prop (Table 1). See Appendix P for full pseudocode.

3.4 Kernel results at long contexts (32k)

We evaluate decode-step attention kernel latency together with end-task accuracy in the long-context decoding regime. Within this section, SDPA is used for prefill and only the decode step uses S2S^{2}ANTA. Kernel timings are reported for a single decoding step on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPU (batch size 1) using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Meta AI, 2024) tensor shapes; we compare against optimized FlashInfer and FlashDecoding backends. The measurement protocol and tensor layouts are provided in Appendix Q.

To make latency comparisons meaningful, we select one operating point per kernel family as the smallest sample budget SS that matches SDPA accuracy on 32k-token long-context tasks. This yields S=128S{=}128 for S2S^{2}ANTA-prop and S=2048S{=}2048 for S2S^{2}ANTA-flash. These are exactly the configurations that deliver ≈1.5×\approx 1.5\times decode-step attention-kernel speedup in Fig. 4 while matching SDPA within confidence intervals in Table 1.

We next verify that these speedup points preserve long-context accuracy. We evaluate on tasks from RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) using 32,768-token prompts: frequent-word extraction (FWE), needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH), single-hop QA (QA1, derived from SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2018)), and multi-hop QA (QA2, derived from HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018)). Results are shown in Table 1.

At these operating points, the speedups are driven primarily by reduced memory traffic from sparsifying reads of the value matrix VV. For S2S^{2}ANTA-prop, S=128S{=}128 corresponds to extremely sparse value access at 32k contexts (e.g., ≲1.56%\lesssim 1.56\% VV access when accounting for GQA). S2S^{2}ANTA-flash attains comparable speedup, but requires a larger total sample budget because uniform per-tile sampling expends samples on low-mass tiles before the deferred renormalization step (“sample waste”).

These timings are kernel-level improvements; realized end-to-end speedups are subject to Amdahl’s Law and are largest in the memory-bound long-context regime (e.g., nk≳8n_{k}\gtrsim 8k) where KV-cache streaming dominates decode time. While S2S^{2}ANTA is multiplier-free in principle, current GPUs are highly optimized for dense fused multiply-accumulate instructions; we therefore view multiplier-free arithmetic as an additional energy-oriented benefit that may become more pronounced on future hardware.

Additional benchmark results for 8k-token contexts are available in Appendix R.

3.5 Energy considerations

Beyond latency, S2S^{2}ANTA’s design offers two complementary paths to energy reduction. First, sparse memory access reduces value-cache traffic from nkn_{k} to SS rows per query, at accuracy-matching operating points, this corresponds to >>90% reductions in value-stage memory access at 32k contexts. Second, replacing dense multiply-accumulate with gather-and-add eliminates multiplication operations entirely. While our current GPU kernels primarily exploit the first benefit, hardware architectures optimized for sparse, adder-centric computation could realize both. These characteristics make S2S^{2}ANTA a natural fit for emerging AI accelerators where memory bandwidth and multiplier energy are primary constraints.

4 General reasoning & accuracy verification

In this section, we consider SANTA, S2S^{2}ANTA-strat (stratified sampling), and S2S^{2}ANTA-sys (systematic sampling) as mathematical constructions (as in Section 2), validating the methods’ accuracy on GSM8K, MMLU, and long-context benchmarks using PyTorch reference implementations. While demonstrated GPU kernel speedups are for autoregressive decoding, evaluations in this section use SANTA in both prefill and decoding. Since SANTA in principle reduces additions and VV memory access by S/nkS/n_{k} and removes post-softmax multiplies, future addition-centric hardware may enable gains in energy efficiency in the compute-heavy prefill phase; for instance, on modern CMOS, a FP16 multiply typically costs 1.1 pJ vs. 0.4 pJ for an add (Horowitz, 2014).

4.1 GSM8K

We consider Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (“Llama 8B”) (Meta AI, 2024) on the GSM8K dataset as a mathematical reasoning benchmark (Cobbe et al., 2021; OpenAI, 2023). Table 2 provides both accuracy and the average number of tokens (prompt + answer). Because the compute and memory access costs of SANTA are contextualized relative to the sequence length nkn_{k}, these sequence lengths justify the regimes where S≪nkS\ll n_{k} and SANTA is, in principle, cheaper than SDPA in attention’s value stage.

Default SANTA exhibits respectable performance, but variance-reduced S2S^{2}ANTA variants demonstrate superior performance across every sample budget SS. S2S^{2}ANTA implementations approach the accuracy of full SDPA (within 1%) while SS remains shorter than the sequence length nkn_{k}, translating to memory-access savings and FLOP energy savings. In deployment settings where LLM users do not require maximum model performance, the sample budget SS can be tuned to save computation cost. For instance, S2S^{2}ANTA-sys achieves 76.42% accuracy at S=64S=64, which is about 19% of the average sequence length of nk=341n_{k}=341 tokens. For a modest accuracy trade-off compared to SDPA’s 78.06%, S2S^{2}ANTA-sys in principle costs 19% of the additions, 19% of the VV-matrix accesses, and no multiplies.

We provide additional DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) (DeepSeek 7B) results and comparisons to sparse top-k attention in Appendix H.

4.2 MMLU

We further evaluate SANTA on the MMLU benchmark (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Center for AI Safety, 2024), which tests factual recall and general reasoning. MMLU benchmarking observes similar trends as GSM8K, where SANTA virtually recovers baseline accuracy at S=256S=256, which is significantly shorter than the average sequence length nk=417n_{k}=417. S2S^{2}ANTA variants outperform default SANTA across SS budgets of 6464–256256, recovering baseline SDPA accuracy (within 1%) with multiplier-free arithmetic and sparse memory access to rows of VV since S≪nkS\ll n_{k}. Extended results with DeepSeek 7B and top-k comparisons are provided in Appendix H.

4.3 Long context benchmarks

We benchmark SANTA on long-context tasks borrowed from RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) with a prompt length of 8192 tokens. The theoretical benefit of S2S^{2}ANTA’s sparse computation is most stark in this long-context regime. With a budget of S=256S=256 in an 8192-token sequence, 𝑺𝟐\bm{S^{2}}ANTA uses just S/nk=3.125%\bm{S/n_{k}=3.125\%} of the value-stage additions and memory accesses compared to full attention (following Table 8). It achieves this while using no multiplications and recovering baseline SDPA accuracy (within ±1%\pm 1\%) across every task.

For full clarity, when Llama 8B’s grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) with 4 grouped queries is fully accounted for, then memory access to unique rows of VV can in the worst case reach 12.5%12.5\%, which remains extremely sparse. Extended results with top-k comparisons are provided in Appendix H.

5 Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} for sparse key access

SANTA reduces memory access for the value matrix by sampling from the softmax distribution; however, it leaves the score computation (q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}}) intact. As illustrated in Fig. 5, we demonstrate that Bernoulli sampling of the query naturally zeroes out query-irrelevant features, thereby effectively reducing memory access for the key matrix.

We propose representing each query element as an independent Bernoulli variable, allowing the corresponding key feature to be pruned when the sampling probability is low. While this method is applicable to the prefill phase, it induces sparse key access specifically during decoding; therefore, we focus on a single query qq. First, the query vector is normalized as q←q/normq\leftarrow q/\text{norm}, where norm≥maxi⁡|qi|\text{norm}\geq\max_{i}|q_{i}|. This ensures that each element qi∈[−1,1]q_{i}\in[-1,1] can be interpreted as a probability. Next, we estimate the product p=q​K𝖳p=qK^{\mathsf{T}} as:

p^=normB​∑n=1Bq^(n)​K𝖳,\widehat{p}=\frac{\text{norm}}{B}\sum_{n=1}^{B}\widehat{q}^{(n)}K^{\mathsf{T}}, (5)

where BB is the sample count and q^(n)\widehat{q}^{(n)} is a sparse ternary vector constructed via Bernoulli sampling (detailed in Appendix C). The linearity of expectation ensures this estimator is unbiased. Because q^(n)\widehat{q}^{(n)} contains only values in {−1,0,+1}\{-1,0,+1\}, p^\widehat{p} can be computed without multiplications by gathering and accumulating selected rows of K𝖳K^{\mathsf{T}}, followed by normalizing bit shifts for fixed-point representations.

Table 5 shows GSM8K results for Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} applied to BitNet 2B (Ma et al., 2025) for both prefill and decoding. Using B=4B=4 stratified samples nearly recovers the accuracy of standard SDPA for the GSM8K benchmark, although the approximated scores typically have a 30%30\% error (Appendix C.1). This suggests that the q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} product within the highly quantized BitNet 2B architecture can tolerate numerical errors while maintaining strong overall performance.

Crucially, Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} enables sparse access to cached keys, a benefit that is uniquely effective during decoding (the prefill phase requires nearly all features). This is shown in Table 5: with B=4B=4, the model needs only 67.5%67.5\% of key features per head (vs. ∼100%\sim 100\% for prefill), while maintaining accuracy within 2%2\% of the SDPA baseline.

5.1 Mean group query

While Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} effectively prunes irrelevant features for individual heads, Grouped Query Attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023) complicates this by sharing keys and values across multiple heads (e.g., groups of 4 in BitNet). Consequently, the set of accessed features becomes the union of those required by all queries in the group, significantly increasing memory traffic. Table 5 illustrates this effect: with B=4B=4 samples, K𝖳K^{\mathsf{T}} access jumps from 67.5%67.5\% per head to 97.9%97.9\% for the group. To preserve sparsity in this scenario, we propose using a representative query mm for the entire group, defined as the mean of the queries’ absolute values. We then construct the estimator m^\widehat{m} for the mean query mm via Monte Carlo sampling (detailed in Appendix C.2), which stochastically prunes the low-amplitude mean features.

With B=4B=4 samples, m^\widehat{m} contains approximately 15% of zero elements, which allows fetching only 85% of key features for the group (Table 5). The product p=q​K𝖳p=qK^{\mathsf{T}} for each query is finally estimated as:

p^=(m^⊙qm)​K𝖳,\widehat{p}=\big(\widehat{m}\odot\frac{q}{m}\big)K^{\mathsf{T}}, (6)

where ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication. In this scenario, calculating p^\widehat{p} requires normalization by mm to compensate for the bias introduced by the mean group query. As shown in Table 5, the resulting estimator achieves similar accuracy to the single-query configuration while saving 15% of key memory accesses. We employ the mean group query estimator (Eq. 6) in all the following experiments.

5.2 Long context benchmarks

We evaluate our method on long-context tasks using Llama 8B, applying Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} strictly during decoding since prefill requires full feature access. As detailed in Table 6, using B=8B=8 samples reduces key feature access to 72.8%72.8\% for Llama 8B, with minimal accuracy loss (<2%<2\% on NIAH, QA1, and QA2). Furthermore, this experiment highlights that key memory access patterns vary significantly across models. In contrast to Llama 8B, BitNet 2B requires accessing 97.1%97.1\% of features for the same budget (B=8B=8, Table 5), a difference we attribute to distinct query distributions.

5.3 Combining Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} and SANTA

Combining SANTA with Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} enables sparse key–value accesses during decoding while replacing the majority of multiplications with additions. Table 7 shows the accuracy for the GSM8K benchmark using BitNet 2B and B=4B=4 Bernoulli samples for the q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} computation, as the number of SANTA samples SS is varied for the value stage. Using B=4B=4 for queries and S=64S=64 for attention weights almost recovers the SDPA baseline with less than 2%2\% accuracy drop. Critically, this combined approach reduces key access by 15.3%15.3\% and value access by 89.2%89.2\%.

6 Related work

Exact attention kernels and memory-bound decoding. FlashAttention-style kernels optimize IO locality and utilization for exact attention, including decoding-focused variants (Dao et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2025). However, exact decoding still streams essentially the full KV state each step at long contexts. Our approach is complementary: rather than further optimizing a full KV scan, we reduce the amount of KV data accessed at runtime by sparsifying value-cache reads (and, for Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}}, key-feature reads).

Reducing KV footprint and retention. KV quantization/compression reduces bytes per KV element (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024), and weight-only quantization targets model parameters (Frantar et al., 2023; Dettmers et al., 2023). GQA reduces KV size via head sharing (Ainslie et al., 2023). Cache-management methods bound KV growth by evicting or pruning tokens (Tang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023), introducing approximation by permanently discarding state. SANTA and Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} are orthogonal to these approaches: they reduce the number of elements accessed over whatever cache is retained, and therefore can stack with compression, GQA, and eviction.

Approximating attention and sampling vs. truncation. Structured sparsity and low-rank approximations reduce attention cost (often in prefill) (Child et al., 2019; Zaheer et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020). In decoding, candidate selection and query-pruning methods reduce the cost of identifying relevant tokens or approximating q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} (Kitaev et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2025; Ribar et al., 2024). This is where our two methods differ in scope: SANTA operates in the value stage and is orthogonal to score-stage approximations, while Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} is an alternative score-stage estimator that induces feature-sparse key access via stochastic ternary queries. Sampling-based attention approximations have also been explored (Kim & Ko, 2022). A direct deterministic baseline is top-kk attention (Gupta et al., 2021), which reduces value reads by truncation but is biased. In contrast, SANTA provides an unbiased estimator of the post-softmax value aggregation with controllable variance, and we emphasize variance reduction (stratified/systematic sampling) together with GPU kernels that realize measured speedups in the memory-bound decoding regime.

7 Conclusion

Long-context autoregressive decoding is frequently constrained by memory bandwidth due to repeated KV-cache access. We introduced SANTA, a stochastic method that avoids streaming the full value cache by sampling S≪nkS\ll n_{k} value rows from the post-softmax distribution and aggregating them with sparse gather-and-add. SANTA is unbiased for the post-softmax value aggregation, admits practical variance reduction via S2S^{2}ANTA stratified/systematic sampling, and provides a tunable accuracy–latency knob in the sample budget SS. On modern GPUs, our observed speedups primarily come from reducing value-cache bandwidth: our S2S^{2}ANTA kernels achieve up to a 1.5×1.5\times decode-step attention-kernel speedup over FlashInfer/FlashDecoding at 32k-token contexts while retaining baseline performance at modest budgets.

We also proposed Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} sampling as a complementary, forward-looking mechanism for the score stage that reduces key-feature access during decoding via stochastic ternary queries, which can be combined with SANTA to sparsify both branches of attention. Beyond reduced memory bandwidth, the predominantly additive structure of both estimators may also be attractive for future adder-centric hardware and/or prefill, which we leave to future work.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

Let μq:=∑jpq​j​Vj=(A​V)q\mu_{q}:=\sum_{j}p_{qj}V_{j}=(AV)_{q}. Then 𝔼⁡[A​V^qind]=𝔼⁡[A​V^qsys]=μq.\mathbb{E}[\widehat{AV}_{q}^{\mathrm{ind}}]=\mathbb{E}[\widehat{AV}_{q}^{\mathrm{sys}}]=\mu_{q}.

Remark A.5 (Systematic vs. independent).

S2S^{2}ANTA-strat is unbiased and admits a variance-dominance theorem, guaranteeing lower variance than that of i.i.d. sampling with default SANTA (Section A.5). S2S^{2}ANTA-sys is also unbiased, but does not provide tractable variance guarantees; empirically it performs comparably.

Appendix B Vector Bernstein tail for SANTA

Theorem B.1 (Vector Bernstein tail for SANTA).

Assume a uniform almost-sure bound ‖Vj−μq‖2≤Vmax\|V_{j}-\mu_{q}\|_{2}\leq V_{\max} for all jj (hence ‖Xs‖2≤Vmax\|X_{s}\|_{2}\leq V_{\max}). Let vq≜𝔼⁡[‖Vi−μq‖22]=tr⁡(Σq)v_{q}\triangleq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|V_{i}-\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}\right]=\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{q}). Then for all t>0t>0,

Pr⁡(‖A​V^q−μq‖2≥t)≤ 2​exp⁡(−S​t22​(vq+Vmax​t/3)).\Pr\!\left(\bigl\|\widehat{AV}_{q}-\mu_{q}\bigr\|_{2}\geq t\right)\;\leq\;2\exp\!\left(-\frac{S\,t^{2}}{2\,(v_{q}+V_{\max}t/3)}\right).

Equivalently, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

‖A​V^q−μq‖2≤2​vq​log⁡(2/δ)S+2​Vmax​log⁡(2/δ)3​S.\bigl\|\widehat{AV}_{q}-\mu_{q}\bigr\|_{2}\;\leq\;\sqrt{\frac{2\,v_{q}\,\log(2/\delta)}{S}}\;+\;\frac{2V_{\max}\,\log(2/\delta)}{3S}.
Proof sketch.

This is a Hilbert-space (vector) Bernstein inequality: apply Bernstein to the mean of independent, mean-zero, LL-bounded vectors with variance proxy vqv_{q}; see, e.g., Boucheron et al. (2013, Thm. 2.10; see also Cor. 2.11) and Pinelis (1994). ∎

Appendix C Estimating q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} via Bernoulli sampling

We first normalize the query vector as q←q/normq\leftarrow q/\text{norm}, where norm≥maxi⁡|qi|\text{norm}\geq\max_{i}|q_{i}| so that each element qi∈[−1,1]q_{i}\in[-1,1] is interpreted as a probability. Then, we introduce the unbiased query estimator q^\widehat{q} where each element qi^\widehat{q_{i}} is an independent ternary Bernoulli variable:

bi\displaystyle b_{i} ∼Bernoulli​(|qi|),\displaystyle\sim\text{Bernoulli}(|q_{i}|), (8)
qi^\displaystyle\widehat{q_{i}} =bi×sign​(qi)∈{−1,0,+1}.\displaystyle=b_{i}\times\text{sign}(q_{i})\in\{-1,0,+1\}.

Sampling from q^\widehat{q} provides an unbiased estimator for the product p=q​K𝖳p=qK^{\mathsf{T}}:

p^=normB​∑n=1Bq^(n)​K𝖳,\widehat{p}=\frac{\text{norm}}{B}\sum_{n=1}^{B}\widehat{q}^{(n)}K^{\mathsf{T}}, (9)

where q^(n)\widehat{q}^{(n)} is a Bernoulli query vector, and BB is the number of samples.

C.1 Bernoulli q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} error

Fig. 6 shows the scaling of the L2 norm error with the number of samples BB, defined as e=‖p^−p‖2/‖p‖2e=||\widehat{p}-p||_{2}/||p||_{2}. In similar fashion as SANTA, stratified Bernoulli sampling reduces the variance of each independent element pi^\widehat{p_{i}}. The variance scales as O⁡(1/B2)O(1/B^{2}), resulting in an overall L2 norm scaling as O⁡(1/B)O(1/B). For this numerical experiment, which uses a head dimension dk=128d_{k}=128 and a context length nk=1024n_{k}=1024, using only B=4B=4 samples induces a mean L2 norm error of approximately 60%60\% for standard Bernoulli sampling, compared to a much lower 30%30\% for stratified sampling.

C.2 q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} for Grouped Query Attention

To maintain sparse key access when keys share multiple queries, as in GQA, we define a common representative query for the group, such as the mean of the absolute values of the queries:

m\displaystyle m =1|𝒢|​∑g∈𝒢|qg|,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}|}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}|q_{g}|, (10)

where 𝒢\mathcal{G} denotes the query group. We then estimate the mean query using Monte Carlo sampling, after normalizing by norm≥maxi⁡mi\text{norm}\geq\max_{i}m_{i}:

bi\displaystyle b_{i} ∼Bernoulli​(mi/norm)\displaystyle\sim\text{Bernoulli}(m_{i}/\text{norm}) (11)
m^\displaystyle\widehat{m} =normB​∑n=1Bb(n)\displaystyle=\frac{\text{norm}}{B}\sum_{n=1}^{B}b^{(n)} (12)

where b(n)b^{(n)} are Bernoulli query vectors with independent elements bib_{i}. After fetching the corresponding K𝖳K^{\mathsf{T}} rows corresponding to non-zero elements of m^\widehat{m}, the product p=q​K𝖳p=qK^{\mathsf{T}} for each query is estimated as:

p^=(m^⊙qm)​K𝖳,\widehat{p}=\big(\widehat{m}\odot\frac{q}{m}\big)K^{\mathsf{T}}, (13)

where ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication. In this mean group query scenario, calculating p^\widehat{p} requires multiplications by the original query qq and normalization by mm to compensate for the bias introduced by the mean query approximation.

Appendix D Empirical variance

To further validate our results, we empirically measure the variance of SANTA, S2S^{2}ANTA-strat, and S2S^{2}ANTA-sys. We sweep the sample budget SS on 8k-token single-hop QA prompts, averaged across model layers and 30 prompts (normalized per head). S2S^{2}ANTA variants exhibit significantly lower variance than SANTA. Though systematic sampling admits no tractable theoretical variance guarantees, it empirically demonstrates similar variance to independent stratified sampling (and requires 1 random number per query instead of SS random numbers). On a log-log scale, slopes for SANTA, S2S^{2}ANTA-strat, and S2S^{2}ANTA-sys are −1.1-1.1, −1.27-1.27, and −1.29-1.29, respectively, matching the 1/S1/S scaling prescribed by theory (see Appendix M for details regarding the measurement protocol).

Appendix E Theoretical operations and memory accesses in autoregressive decoding

Table 8 displays the theoretical additions, multiplications, and memory accesses incurred by SANTA in the value stage of attention, where the attention scores AA multiply VV. The score computation q​K𝖳qK^{\mathsf{T}} is similar for both SANTA and SDPA, and is therefore omitted in this analysis (see Appendix G). We count individual scalar elements which are added together, multiplied together, or accessed by memory. Architecture-dependent effects such as multiply-accumulate (MAC) instructions, caching effects, or operation parallelism are not accounted for; arguments are fundamental and hardware-agnostic.

By virtue of SANTA’s sparsity, SANTA demonstrates a S/nkS/n_{k} reduction in post-softmax additions and reads to rows of VV, where SS is the sample budget and nkn_{k} is the number of keys (sequence length). A key distinction is that SANTA costs fewer additions than SDPA; SANTA does not seek to replace the multiplications in the A​VAV computation, but rather, leverages sparse sampling to decrease the total number of additions while eliminating multiplications. So long as S≪nkS\ll n_{k}, the advantage of attention sparsity holds true. Sampling overhead is not included; it is highly dependent on implementation, but drawing S≪nkS\ll n_{k} samples should be lightweight relative to memory accesses, multiplies, and adds (indeed, this proves to be the case with GPU kernel latency demonstrations in Section 3).

Whereas SDPA incurs nk​dkn_{k}d_{k} multiplications from computing dot products, SANTA only costs dkd_{k} normalizing multiplies by 1/S1/S. dkd_{k} is a constant model parameter and does not increase with the sequence length nkn_{k}. Furthermore, if SS is chosen as a power of 2 and the model has a fixed point representation, this normalization may be implemented as a bit-shift.

In prefill, while similar arguments hold for SANTA’s reduced additions and multiplies, there is no longer sparse memory access to the value matrix VV. Each of nqn_{q} queries may each sample SS rows of VV, therefore requiring ≫S\gg S rows of VV when the union across all queries is considered (see Appendices F, G).

Appendix F Unique VV-row coverage for SANTA prefill

Table 9 shows the percentage of unique VV rows read by SANTA during prefill passes of differing sequence lengths nkn_{k}. Standard Gaussian distributed inputs Q,K,VQ,K,V are passed into SANTA with dk=128d_{k}=128 and H=32H=32 heads for multi-headed attention. Even in the long-context, S≪nkS\ll n_{k} regime, any appreciable number of samples SS results in SANTA sampling most rows of VV when the union across all queries is considered. For S=16S=16, selected sequence lengths from nk=1​k−16​kn_{k}=1k-16k show SANTA reading almost all (>94%>94\%) rows of VV, because each of nq=nkn_{q}=n_{k} queries stochastically attend to SS sampled keys. Therefore, while SANTA features sparse VV access during autoregressive decoding, SANTA does not have apparent benefit from sparse memory access in prefill. Arguments concerning SANTA’s reduced addition and multiplication operations are still valid in prefill (Table 10).

Appendix G Theoretical operations and memory accesses in prefill

While SANTA’s apparent memory sparsity benefits are most viable in autoregressive decoding, for full clarity, this section provides generalized analysis for prefill. We consider the computational cost of SANTA, SDPA, and top-k attention, focusing on FLOPs and memory traffic in the value stage. Table 10 summarizes the theoretical costs per attention head. For the score stage (Q​K𝖳QK^{\mathsf{T}}), the “Reads” entry (nq+nk)​dk(n_{q}+n_{k})d_{k} counts each query and key vector once per head, assuming they are loaded once from DRAM and then reused in on-chip memory during the matmul. In contrast, for the value stage we report nq​nk​dkn_{q}n_{k}d_{k}, nq​k​dkn_{q}kd_{k}, and nq​S​dkn_{q}Sd_{k} for dense SDPA, top-kk, and SANTA, respectively, which count the per-query accesses rather than unique loads of elements from memory.

While top-kk attention is memory-efficient and generally performs well, it introduces bias and can degrade significantly when the attention distribution is heavy-tailed. For example, recent work (Chen et al., 2025) shows that tasks such as common word extraction suffer when relevant information is not concentrated in the top-kk entries. In contrast, stochastic estimators like SANTA provide an unbiased estimate of full attention and retain robustness in such cases.

For both top-k and SANTA, we define a notion of compute budget, where kk is the number of keys selected by top-k for each query of each attention head, while SS is a sample budget representing the number of samples that SANTA draws for each query of each attention head. By default, we employ uniform SS across model layers, though ablations suggest that SS can be optimized per layer (Appendix I, J).

We omit softmax computation, top-kk sorting overhead, and sampling from this analysis, as they are lightweight relative to memory accesses and the VV matrix multiply, and are highly implementation-dependent. For example, many implementations use partial sorting (Samaga B L et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025).

In both FLOPs and memory reads, SDPA scales as nq​nkn_{q}n_{k}, reflecting the cost of full quadratic attention computation. Both top-kk and SANTA reduce this to nq​kn_{q}k and nq​Sn_{q}S, respectively, assuming fixed budgets with k,S≪nkk,S\ll n_{k}. This shifts the overall complexity of the value stage from quadratic to linear in sequence length, given a fixed budget kk or SS.

Top-kk still incurs multiplication costs while SANTA eliminates multiplies. Top-kk performs nq​k​dkn_{q}kd_{k} multiplications (per head), while SANTA requires only nq​dkn_{q}d_{k} divisions for normalization (if SS is chosen as a power of 2, even these few divisions become simple bit-shifts).

Appendix H Additional DeepSeek and top-k results

Tables 11,  12,  13, and  14 feature additional GSM8K and MMLU results with comparisons using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and top-k attention. Table  15 exhibits long-context benchmark results identical to Table 4, except with additional top-k comparisons.

Comparing SANTA and top-k requires care, as they have different computational profiles. We present results for sample budget SS equal to the top-kk budget kk not as an iso-compute benchmark, but to demonstrate that SANTA achieves comparable or superior accuracy while using a fundamentally cheaper set of operations. At S=kS=k: top-kk costs nq​k​dkn_{q}kd_{k} multiplications + nq​k​dkn_{q}kd_{k} additions, whereas SANTA costs 0 multiplications + nq​S​dkn_{q}Sd_{k} additions (Table 10).

A 32-bit FP multiply costs 3.7 pJ versus 0.9 pJ for addition (Horowitz, 2014). For equal budgets k=Sk=S, the value-stage energy consumption for the two methods are approximately: k×(3.7+0.9)=4.6​kk\times(3.7+0.9)=4.6k pJ per element for top-k, vs. S×0.9=0.9​SS\times 0.9=0.9S pJ per element for SANTA. Relative to top-k, SANTA yields an ≈5×\approx 5\times energy reduction for value-stage FLOPs. We acknowledge that these are approximate energy estimates; we aim to provide hardware-agnostic comparisons, as modern GPU hardware is optimized for matmuls and contiguous memory access, while SANTA involves adds and sparse memory access.

Regarding memory accesses: SANTA’s accesses to elements of the VV matrix scale as nq​S​dkn_{q}Sd_{k}, which in the worst case matches top-k’s nq​k​dkn_{q}kd_{k} memory accesses at k=Sk=S. However, since SANTA samples with replacement, the number of unique keys is ≤S\leq S. In practice, as we quantify in Appendix L, the number of unique keys sampled is <S<S, which may offer significant caching advantages.

For benchmarking, we apply SANTA and top-k to both prefill and autoregressive decoding. However, in practice, these sparse attention implementations may see greater benefit during decoding, when only a single query sparsely selects rows of VV.

SANTA variants demonstrate strong performance relative to top-k on GSM8K and MMLU benchmarks, despite SANTA requiring no multiplications and a similar number of additions and memory accesses for k=Sk=S. However, the most remarkable result is shown in Table 15, where S2S^{2}ANTA variants outperform top-k across virtually every long-context task for all k=Sk=S. S2S^{2}ANTA’s lead over top-k is most apparent for multi-hop question answering (QA2), where S2S^{2}ANTA variants lead in performance by ≈5%\approx 5\% in several cases. It is plausible that long context tasks — multi-hop QA in particular — have information that is not concentrated in the top-k keys, and therefore SANTA’s unbiased estimate of attention outperforms top-k, which drops information and cannot attend to keys outside of the kk largest attention scores.

Appendix I Ablation study: one-hot attention samples

This section probes a fundamental question: how much does each attention layer matter? We find that one-hot stochastic attention, a limiting case of SANTA with S=1S=1, acts as a surprisingly sharp diagnostic. It reveals which transformer layers are robust to severe approximation and which are not, offering a practical lens into where attention precision matters most.

We perform these ablations by setting S=1S=1 in a single layer while keeping all other layers at fixed sample budgets: S=16S=16 for DeepSeek 7B (28 layers) and S=256S=256 for Llama 8B (32 layers). In this setting, each query attends to only one randomly sampled key, making that layer a hard attention bottleneck.

Models are evaluated on GSM8K and MMLU with the same protocol as Tables 2 and 3. The effect of this localized bottleneck on accuracy is summarized in Fig. 8. Some layers exhibit almost no degradation when ablated in this way, while others collapse entirely, most notably middle layers in DeepSeek 7B and the first layer in Llama 8B.

In DeepSeek 7B, layers 12–18 are highly sensitive to approximation, while early and final layers are much more tolerant. In contrast, Llama 8B exhibits extreme sensitivity in just the first layer. These patterns suggest that attention importance is neither uniform nor trivially architectural.

We observe similar qualitative trends regardless of the baseline sample budget; the S=16S=16 and S=256S=256 settings are arbitrary. The early-layer sensitivity in Llama 8B is consistent with prior findings on high-entropy attention in shallow layers (Clark et al., 2019), and with prior work that avoids approximating early layers (Tang et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024). The middle-layer fragility in DeepSeek 7B remains an open and intriguing observation.

Appendix J Layer-wise sample budget through RL

We now consider a global sample budget shared across all 28 transformer layers of DeepSeek 7B, allowing each layer to have a distinct sample count. We optimize this allocation using a REINFORCE-style algorithm (Williams, 1992), detailed in Algorithm 1.

We train the policy on the GSM8K training set. The policy logits 𝜽∈ℝ28\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{28} define a softmax distribution over layers. At each iteration, we sample schedules using a multinomial draw over this distribution, with a total budget of 224 samples (i.e., 8×288\times 28). Each episode evaluates 16 questions; the reward is the fraction answered correctly. We intentionally starve the baseline with S=8S=8 samples per layer to create room for the learned schedule to improve.

Fig. 9 shows the final learned schedule after 501 iterations. The allocation aligns strikingly with the ablation trends from Fig. 8: more samples are assigned to the first and middle layers, where one-hot attention was most detrimental. That REINFORCE independently rediscovers this structure from only reward signals confirms that these patterns are not artifacts of the ablation method but instead are intrinsic to the models.

This experiment is not tuned for peak accuracy, but demonstrates that adaptive per-layer budgets meaningfully outperform fixed ones. Please see Appendix K for implementation details of distributed reinforcement learning using a Kubernetes compute cluster.

Appendix K Distributed reinforcement learning on Kubernetes

Topology.

All pods mount a single read–write volume that serves as the rendezvous point.

  • •

    Aggregator pod. Holds the current policy and records a running history of baselines and gradients.

  • •

    Worker pods. Operate in a tight loop: (i) read the latest policy; (ii) sample a 28-dimensional schedule; (iii) evaluate ten batches of 16 questions; (iv) append a small JSON-lines result file to a designated “inbox” directory on the volume.

Aggregator loop.

Whenever at least one new result file appears, the aggregator moves all current files into a private folder for the next iteration, computes the REINFORCE update and writes a new policy snapshot. It never pauses or signals the workers; it simply processes whatever has arrived. In practice, workers are unlikely to finish evaluation simultaneously, thus nearly every policy update comes from one worker output (10 ×\times 16 questions). If two land together, the aggregator just uses a double-sized batch, which lowers the gradient’s variance.

Asynchrony and fault-tolerance.

  • •

    Workers can be terminated at any time; partial output vanishes harmlessly.

  • •

    Workers always proceed with the newest policy that has reached disk; no locking is needed.

  • •

    If the aggregator restarts it scans the history directory, resumes from the last completed iteration, and continues.

Scaling and resources.

The worker Deployment’s replica count can be scaled up or down at any time during learning. For the 501 iterations in Fig. 9 we ran 50 GPU workers on a mix of RTX 3090, L4, and A10 cards (24 GB Ampere generation cards) for roughly 20 hours, totaling ≈1000\approx 1000 GPU-hours. The aggregator requests just one CPU core and a few hundred MiB of RAM.

Terminology.

We keep the names aggregator and worker to highlight the simple “parameter-server” flavor of the design, but these roles align exactly with the common learner/actor split in distributed reinforcement learning.

Appendix L Unique key-count

Since all versions of SANTA sample keys with replacement, the number of unique keys may be less than the sample budget SS. In Table 17, we empirically measure the average number of unique keys sampled by the last query position for 8192-token single-hop QA prompts (normalized per head and averaged across model layers). This is indicative of the key diversity observed in autoregressive decoding. For a given SS, S2S^{2}ANTA variants achieve higher key diversity than default SANTA. Furthermore, the number of unique keys tends to be ≪S\ll S, implying that fewer than SS unique rows of VV require memory accesses. See Appendix M for details about the measurement protocol.

Appendix M Implementation & measurement protocol for empirical variance and unique keys sampled

Setting.

For a single layer/head at the last prefill position q⋆q^{\star}, let the post-softmax attention over nkn_{k} keys be pj≥0p_{j}\geq 0 with ∑j=1nkpj=1\sum_{j=1}^{n_{k}}p_{j}=1, and let Vj∈ℝdkV_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} denote the corresponding value vectors. The dense-attention mean is

μ=∑j=1nkpj​Vj∈ℝdk.\mu\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{n_{k}}p_{j}\,V_{j}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}.

SANTA estimator.

Given a per-head sampling budget SS, all SANTA variants estimate μ\mu with

A​V^=1S​∑s=1SVJs,\widehat{AV}\;=\;\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}V_{J_{s}},

where the key indices {Js}\{J_{s}\} are drawn by one of three schemes: (i) multinomial; (ii) independent equal-mass stratified; or (iii) systematic (random-start, fixed-stride). These are the same variants used in the main paper; the code paths that implement them also record the per-head statistics described below at q⋆q^{\star}.

M.1 What we measure (per head at q⋆q^{\star})

(1) Unique keys.

The number of distinct keys touched by the sampler,

U:=|{J1,…,JS}|,U\;:=\;\big|\{J_{1},\dots,J_{S}\}\big|,

upper-bounded by SS (can be <S<S if high-probability keys repeat). This is a proxy for how many memory locations each head actually reads.

(2) Variance trace of the estimator.

We report the trace of the covariance (expected squared ℓ2\ell_{2} error) of A​V^\widehat{AV},

VarTrace⁡(A​V^):=𝔼⁡[‖A​V^−μ‖22]=tr⁡(Cov⁡(A​V^)),\operatorname{VarTrace}(\widehat{AV})\;:=\;\mathbb{E}\big[\|\widehat{AV}-\mu\|_{2}^{2}\big]\;=\;\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\mathrm{Cov}(\widehat{AV})\right),

specialized to each sampling scheme:

  • •

    Multinomial (closed form). Let Σ:=∑j=1nkpj​(Vj−μ)​(Vj−μ)⊤\Sigma:=\sum_{j=1}^{n_{k}}p_{j}\,(V_{j}-\mu)(V_{j}-\mu)^{\top} so that tr⁡(Σ)=∑jpj​‖Vj‖22−‖μ‖22\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j}p_{j}\|V_{j}\|_{2}^{2}-\|\mu\|_{2}^{2}. Then

    VarTracemulti⁡(A​V^)=1S​tr⁡(Σ).\operatorname{VarTrace}_{\mathrm{multi}}(\widehat{AV})\;=\;\frac{1}{S}\,\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma).
  • •

    Independent equal-mass stratified (closed form). Partition [0,1)[0,1) into SS equal strata; for each stratum mm, form the within-stratum discrete distribution induced by pp and let Σm\Sigma_{m} be the corresponding value covariance. Because draws across strata are independent,

    VarTracestrat⁡(A​V^)=1S2​∑m=0S−1tr⁡(Σm).\operatorname{VarTrace}_{\mathrm{strat}}(\widehat{AV})\;=\;\frac{1}{S^{2}}\sum_{m=0}^{S-1}\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{m}).
  • •

    Systematic (replicate-based estimate). There is no general closed form that holds uniformly for systematic sampling, so we estimate variance by repeated random starts. With R≥2R\geq 2 independent offsets, we compute A​V^(r)\widehat{AV}^{(r)} for each replicate, then use

    VarTrace^sys​(A​V^)\displaystyle\widehat{\operatorname{VarTrace}}_{\mathrm{sys}}(\widehat{AV}) =1R−1​∑r=1R‖A​V^(r)−V¯‖22,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\big\|\widehat{AV}^{(r)}-\overline{V}\big\|_{2}^{2},
    V¯\displaystyle\overline{V} =1R​∑r=1RA​V^(r).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\widehat{AV}^{(r)}.

    This estimator is applied per head at q⋆q^{\star}.

M.2 How we aggregate and report

For each prompt, we compute UU and the variance-trace scalar per head at q⋆q^{\star}, then average over heads within a layer, average over layers, and finally average over prompts to obtain the quantities reported in the variance plots:

U¯​(S,variant)andT¯​(S,variant)=VarTrace¯​(A​V^).\overline{U}(S,\text{variant})\quad\text{and}\quad\overline{T}(S,\text{variant})\;=\;\overline{\operatorname{VarTrace}}(\widehat{AV}).

This yields the curves summarized in the main text as a function of the budget SS and the SANTA variant.

Protocol summary.

All measurements use evaluation-mode forward passes, prefill-only, and record statistics at the last token per head; no additional dense attention pass is performed to form empirical errors. For multinomial and stratified we use the exact formulas above; for systematic we use the replicate-based estimator.

Appendix N Prompting, Parsing, and Grading

In Section 4.1, we evaluate the GSM8K test split (1319 prompts) 3 times. Evaluation code uses straightforward answer parsing and borrows grading code from PRM800K (Lightman et al., 2024). For all runs, temperature=0.6\text{temperature}=0.6, top-p=0.95\text{top-p}=0.95, and repetition penalty=1.1\text{repetition penalty}=1.1. We use left-padded batches of 8–16 prompts.

In Section 4.2, we average results over three runs on the MMLU validation set (1531 questions), using identical decoding parameters as GSM8K.

In Section 4.3, long-context benchmark results are averaged over 500 prompts and greedy decoding is employed with no repetition penalty applied.

DeepSeek 7B + GSM8K

Aspect Procedure
Prompt Question, blank line, then Please reason step by step, and put your final numeric answer within \boxed{}.
Answer extraction Perform a brace-balanced search for the last occurrence of \boxed{…} (robust to nested braces). If none is found, fall back to the final ∼\sim200 characters of the model output.
Grading Numeric equality judged by the MIT-licensed PRM800K grader; every prompt is counted, and blank or unparsable predictions score 0.

DeepSeek 7B + MMLU

Aspect Procedure
Prompt Question, four labeled choices, then Answer briefly. Put your final answer as a single letter inside \boxed{}.
Answer extraction Brace-balanced search for the last occurrence of \boxed{…}; if none is found, inspect the final ∼\sim300 characters of the output. Scan this region backwards and take the first occurrence of A–D (case-insensitive), then convert it to uppercase.
Grading The predicted letter is compared with the gold key (case-insensitive). If no valid letter is found—or the output is blank—the item scores 0; otherwise it scores 1 when the letters match.

Llama 8B + GSM8K

Aspect Procedure
Prompt Meta chat template. System: “You are a precise mathematician. Explain your reasoning step by step, then output ONLY the final number on a new line.” User: the GSM8K question.
Answer extraction Inspect the model reply in order: (i) the last non-empty line of the response; (ii) if that fails, the final 25 whitespace-separated tokens. From the selected chunk, take the first integer-looking token (commas allowed, optional leading minus).
Grading Numeric equality judged by the MIT-licensed PRM800K grader; every question is counted, and blank or unparsable answers score 0.

Llama 8B + MMLU

Aspect Procedure
Prompt Meta chat template. System: “You are a knowledgeable and concise subject-matter expert. Work through the problem step by step. Finally, on a new line, output ONLY the single capital letter (A, B, C, or D) that corresponds to the correct choice.” User: the question followed by the four labeled choices A–D.
Answer extraction Take the substring after the last newline and scan it left-to-right for the first capital A–D (case-insensitive). If none is found, inspect the final 10 whitespace-separated tokens of the whole response, scanning them right-to-left for A–D.
Grading Predicted letter (upper-cased) is compared with the gold key. Every question is counted; if no valid letter is found or it does not match the gold answer, the item scores 0.

Llama 8B + RULER prompts

Aspect Procedure
Prompt Prompts are generated for the following RULER sub-tasks with a length of 4096–32768 tokens: fwe, niah_multivalue, qa_1, and qa_2. Greedy decoding is used. The model generates a maximum of 64 new tokens.
Grading fwe: partial credit = (# of gold words present in the model output) / 3 (case-insensitive set match). niah_multivalue: take the first four unique integers from the model output; partial credit = (# of these that appear in the gold set) / 4. qa_1 and qa_2: correct if the gold answer string appears as a case-insensitive substring of the model output.

Appendix Q Decode-step kernel microbenchmark details

This appendix describes the microbenchmark used to measure decode-step attention latency for FlashAttention2 decoding (“FlashDecoding”), FlashInfer decoding, and our custom S2S^{2}ANTA CUDA kernels. The intent is to be explicit about tensor shapes, software/hardware environment, cache state, and what is (and is not) included in the reported runtimes, in order to support a fair comparison.

What is being measured.

We measure GPU kernel time for a single decoding step (one new token) as a function of the KV-cache length nkn_{k}. Timing is performed with CUDA events, recorded on the active CUDA stream and synchronized on the end event each iteration. The reported milliseconds therefore reflect elapsed time on the GPU timeline for the CUDA work launched by a single backend call (which may internally launch multiple kernels). All Python/CPU overhead and input construction are excluded by allocating and populating tensors outside the timed region and recording events immediately around the backend call.

Hardware and driver.

All measurements were run on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPU (48 GB). The installed driver reported by nvidia-smi was 580.82.07 (CUDA compatibility reported as 13.0).

Software environment (versions).

The benchmark environment used:

  • •

    PyTorch 2.6.0+cu124

  • •

    flash-attn 2.7.3 (FlashAttention2)

  • •

    flashinfer-python 0.5.3

Our S2S^{2}ANTA kernels are invoked through a PyTorch CUDA extension (custom CUDA code callable from PyTorch); the timed region includes all CUDA kernels launched by this extension entrypoint.

Decode geometry and tensor shapes.

We benchmark a single-batch decode step with head geometry matching a Llama-style GQA configuration:

H=32,Hkv=8,dk=128,G=H/Hkv=4,H=32,\quad H_{\mathrm{kv}}=8,\quad d_{k}=128,\quad G=H/H_{\mathrm{kv}}=4,

where HH is the number of query heads, HkvH_{\mathrm{kv}} is the number of KV heads, and dkd_{k} is the head dimension. The query length is one token (decode), batch size is one, and attention is causal.

For each cache length nkn_{k}, the following tensors are constructed once and reused across timing iterations:

  • •

    Query tensor with shape [H,dk][H,d_{k}].

  • •

    Key/value cache tensors stored in a sequence-major layout with shape [nk+1,Hkv,dk][n_{k}{+}1,H_{\mathrm{kv}},d_{k}]. (The extra +1+1 slot corresponds to the current token.)

All backends are run with the same causal setting and the standard softmax scaling 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_{k}}, with dropout disabled.

Input distribution and dtype.

All inputs are i.i.d. Gaussian (torch.randn) generated directly on the GPU. Unless otherwise stated, the query, keys, and values are provided in bfloat16 (the harness also supports fp16). A fixed RNG seed is used so that, for a given nkn_{k}, each backend sees the same input tensors.

Cold-cache protocol (L2 thrashing).

To reduce sensitivity to favorable cache residency effects: before each timed iteration, we touch a large GPU buffer by performing an in-place update on a 512 MB float32 tensor. This operation is intended to thrash GPU caches (including L2) via a large read+write stream. The cache-thrash operation is executed outside the timed region (before the start event is recorded), and therefore is not included in the reported kernel time.

Timing protocol and trial structure.

For each cache length nkn_{k} and each backend, we run a fixed number of warmup and timed iterations:

  • •

    Warmup: 10 untimed iterations to amortize one-time effects (e.g., kernel selection/caching inside libraries).

  • •

    Timing: 40 timed iterations. Each iteration performs an optional cache-thrash (not timed), then records a start CUDA event, launches the backend once, records an end CUDA event, synchronizes on the end event, and reads elapsed milliseconds from the event pair.

  • •

    Aggregation: we report the mean latency over the 40 timed iterations.

All tensor allocations and concatenations/appends used to construct inputs are performed outside the timed region.

Note on KV-cache appends in FlashDecoding.

FlashAttention2 decoding performs a fused KV-cache append/update as part of its decode call, whereas FlashInfer decoding and our S2S^{2}ANTA decode kernels do not perform an internal append in this benchmark. To isolate the attention-like decode computation for FlashInfer and S2S^{2}ANTA, we provide a cache tensor that already includes the current token in the preallocated [nk+1,Hkv,dk][n_{k}{+}1,H_{\mathrm{kv}},d_{k}] storage.

This asymmetry is not material in the long-context regime: the fused append cost is O⁡(Hkv​dk)O(H_{\mathrm{kv}}d_{k}) per step and does not scale with nkn_{k}, so its fractional contribution decreases as nkn_{k} grows. Our speedup comparisons focus on large KV-cache lengths (e.g., 8k–32k tokens), where the attention computation dominates. Including the fused append inside FlashDecoding therefore does not change qualitative conclusions in this regime (and makes the FlashDecoding measurement slightly more conservative relative to an “attention-only” timing).

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
